_note: DRAFT launch set. Every entry is draft until the owner has reviewed it. Wording is my own. The sources listed are references to consult: none has yet been checked against two independent sources (sourcesChecked is false until that is done). Labels: Fact = a checkable date or event; Tradition = a custom reported in Ireland; Saying = a proverb, not tied to the date it sits on.

entries.title: Oíche Shamhna, Hallowe'en
entries.text: Hallowe'en, Oíche Shamhna, was kept with feasting and games, including fortune-telling games about marriage. A barmbrack had small tokens baked into it, such as a ring, and turnips were hollowed out as lanterns before pumpkins took over.
entries.someplacessay: The foods, games and tokens in the brack differed from place to place.
sources: National Museum of Ireland, Irish Folklife Collections: 'Traditions and customs of Halloween / Samhain', https://www.museum.ie/en-ie/collections-research/folklife-collections/folklife-collections-list-(1)/religion-and-calendar-customs/hallowe-en-samhain (read on the museum's source.museum.ie mirror), checked 2026-11-03

Aoife McElwain, 'Tricks, treats and dead souls: Halloween habits and food traditions', The Irish Times, 31 Oct 2016, https://www.irishtimes.com/life-and-style/food-and-drink/tricks-treats-and-dead-souls-halloween-habits-and-food-traditions-1.2847317, checked 2026-11-03
entries.checkNote: Fires dropped: neither source mentions Samhain bonfires. Museum and Irish Times support feasting, games, marriage divination, brack with a ring, turnip lanterns (a 19th-century turnip lantern is in the Museum of Country Life).

entries.title: Samhain
entries.text: Samhain, 1 November, was the first day of winter in the old Irish calendar, and one of the four old quarter days. The main celebrations took place on the evening before.
entries.someplacessay: Some older accounts keep the festival on the evening of 31 October, since the old day was counted from nightfall.
sources: National Museum of Ireland, Irish Folklife Collections: 'Traditions and customs of Halloween / Samhain', https://www.museum.ie/en-ie/collections-research/folklife-collections/folklife-collections-list-(1)/religion-and-calendar-customs/hallowe-en-samhain (via source.museum.ie), checked 2026-11-03
Foclóir Gaeilge-Béarla (Ó Dónaill), Foras na Gaeilge, entry 'Samhain', https://www.teanglann.ie/en/fgb/Samhain, checked 2026-11-03
entries.checkNote: Removed 'the year began here': neither source says it, so it needs a third source or stays out. Museum: first day of winter, marked 1 November, celebrated the evening before. Dictionary: Samhain is the ancient festival of 1 November. 'One of four quarter days' is from the README, not these sources.

entries.title: Lá na Marbh, All Souls' Day
entries.text: 2 November is All Souls' Day, the Church's day for praying for the dead, and the Church in Ireland dedicates the whole month of November to remembering them. Parishes mark it with prayers, remembrance services and the blessing of graves.
entries.someplacessay: Customs differ by parish and by family.
sources: Irish Catholic Bishops' Conference, 'In November We Remember', 27 Oct 2020, https://www.catholicbishops.ie/2020/10/27/in-november-we-remember-2/, checked 2026-11-03
Ruadhán Jones, 'November, the month of saints and souls', The Irish Catholic, 12 Nov 2020, https://www.irishcatholic.com/november-the-month-of-saints-and-souls/, checked 2026-11-03
entries.checkNote: The draft said parishes read out names through November and that the dead were also remembered the night before. Neither is supported (sources mention a remembrance space in church, blessing of graves, services). Both sources are Catholic Church voices, so this is the church custom, not a folklore archive account.

entries.title: Níl aon tinteán mar do thinteán féin
entries.text: A well-known proverb: there is no hearth like your own hearth, meaning there is no place like home. It suits these early dark evenings. It is not tied to this date.
entries.someplacessay: The wording varies a little from place to place.
sources: Foclóir Gaeilge-Béarla (Ó Dónaill), Foras na Gaeilge, entry 'tinteán' (gives the proverb 'Níl aon tinteán mar do thinteán féin', glossed 'there is no place like home'), https://www.teanglann.ie/en/fgb/tinte%C3%A1n, checked 2026-11-03
[second source still needed] Foras na Gaeilge, New English-Irish Dictionary, https://www.focloir.ie/en/dictionary/ei/hearth confirms tinteán = hearth only, not the proverb, checked 2026-11-03
entries.checkNote: Only one source (Ó Dónaill) gives the proverb itself. A printed proverb collection with page number is needed for the second; I could not read one. sourcesChecked stays false.

entries.title: Oíche Fhéile Mártain, St Martin's Eve
entries.text: On St Martin's Eve, 10 November, a fowl or other animal was killed at the door in many districts, and its blood sprinkled at the threshold and corners of the house to keep out harm. Work with wheels, such as spinning or milling, was avoided on the day.
entries.someplacessay: The custom was found from north Connacht to Kerry and across the midlands, and was rarer in Ulster and on the east coast. It could be kept on the eve or on 11 November itself.
sources: Marion McGarry, 'Opinion: Blood sacrifice and rites in Ireland on 11 November', RTÉ Brainstorm, 8 Nov 2019, https://rte.ie/brainstorm/2019/1108/1089533-martinmas-blood-sacrifice-rites-ireland-november-11th (cites Kevin Danaher, The Year in Ireland, and Henry Morris in Béaloideas), checked 2026-11-03

Máirtín Mac Con Iomaire, 'Martinmas: saints, spiders' webs, pagan pasts and prophylactics', The Irish Times, 9 Nov 2020, https://www.irishtimes.com/culture/heritage/martinmas-saints-spiders-webs-pagan-pasts-and-prophylactics-1.4404711, checked 2026-11-03; also 'November 11th - Martinmas in Co. Mayo', https://www.mayo-ireland.ie/en/about-mayo/arts-culture/folklore/martinmas.html
entries.checkNote: Draft said strongest in the south and east: wrong. Sources say north Connacht to Kerry and the midlands, rarer on the east coast. Both articles draw on Danaher and Mac Fhloinn's 'Blood Rite' so they are not fully independent; the Mayo page is a third local confirmation. The RTÉ title is approximate. Blood-sacrifice detail is strong; check you are happy to show it.

entries.title: The Feast of the Immaculate Conception
entries.text: 8 December, the Feast of the Immaculate Conception, was a holy day, and for generations it was the traditional day for people from the country to go to Dublin and other towns for their Christmas shopping. The habit has faded in recent years.
entries.someplacessay: As a holy day, schools were closed, which let families make a day of it. Some people still count it as the start of the Christmas season, others do not.
sources: Una Mullally, 'December 8th: The day when people "from the country" came to Dublin to shop', The Irish Times, 8 Dec 2019, https://www.irishtimes.com/culture/heritage/december-8th-the-day-when-people-from-the-country-came-to-dublin-to-shop-1.4094195, checked 2026-11-03

Marion McGarry, Irish Christmas traditions feature, RTÉ Brainstorm, https://www.rte.ie/brainstorm/2024/1209/1265469-christmas-traditions-ireland-december-8th-margadh-mor-christmas-box-american-letter (quotes Lillis Ó Laoire), checked 2026-11-03
entries.checkNote: Draft said 'nearest town'; both sources say Dublin and city shopping in particular. Past tense for 'still known as': the Irish Times piece says it used to mark the start of the season. Both are journalism, not a social-history study.

entries.title: Grianstad an Gheimhridh, winter solstice
entries.text: The shortest day of the year. At Newgrange in County Meath, a beam of the rising sun runs down the passage and lights the inner chamber around the winter solstice, through a gap called the roof-box.
entries.someplacessay: The sunlight reaches the chamber on several mornings around the solstice, 19 to 23 December, not only on the day itself. The solstice falls on 21 or 22 December depending on the year.
sources: National Museum of Ireland, 'The Winter solstice at Newgrange', https://source.museum.ie/en-IE/Collections-Research/Irish-Antiquities-Division-Collections/Irish-Antiquities-Articles/The-Winter-solstice-at-Newgrange (roof-box channels sunlight along the passage at sunrise on the solstice), checked 2026-11-03

Tourism Ireland, 'Newgrange, County Meath', ireland.com, https://www.ireland.com/en/magazine/built-heritage/newgrange/ (light travels 19 metres up the passage); solstice dates from the U.S. Naval Observatory seasons service, https://aa.usno.navy.mil/api/seasons (see README); 19-23 December from newgrange.com/solstice-lottery.htm, checked 2026-11-03
entries.checkNote: Roof-box added. 'Several days' (19 to 23 December) came from newgrange.com, a private site, because gov.ie blocked me and no heritageireland.ie page was found. Worth a look at heritageireland.ie by hand.

entries.title: Oíche Nollag, Christmas Eve
entries.text: On Christmas Eve a lit candle was placed in the window, widely explained as a welcome for Mary and Joseph and any traveller looking for shelter. In some accounts the youngest child lights it and someone named Mary puts it out.
entries.someplacessay: Accounts differ: some say the head of the house lights it, and some give it a Penal-times origin (a signal to wandering priests). Some Irish people say they never heard of it.
sources: 'The candle in the window', Kilkenny Observer, https://kilkennyobserver.ie/the-candle-in-the-window/ (welcome to Mary and Joseph, door left unlatched), checked 2026-11-03

Cindy Thomson, 'The Irish Christmas Candle in the Window', The Wild Geese, 12 Dec 2014, https://thewildgeese.irish/xn/detail/6442157:BlogPost:132236 (doubts how widely known it was), checked 2026-11-03; also IrishCentral, https://www.irishcentral.com/roots/christmas-ireland-history-traditions
entries.checkNote: Draft claimed a name rule and youngest child as fact: only popular articles support it, and one author found Irish people who had never heard of it. Marked as a reported custom. No folklore archive or museum source found: Dúchas returned a security check page to my fetcher, so I did not go round it. sourcesChecked false until a folklore source is found.

entries.title: Ar scáth a chéile a mhaireann na daoine
entries.text: A well-loved proverb, often translated as people live in each other's shelter. It fits Christmas Day, when many people open their doors to others. It is not tied to this date.
entries.someplacessay: People translate it in different ways, such as 'we live in each other's shadow' or 'in each other's shelter'.
sources: An Irish proverbs collection (to check)
An English-Irish dictionary entry for scáth (to check)

entries.title: Lá an Dreoilín, St Stephen's Day
entries.text: Traditionally, groups of wren boys went from house to house on St Stephen's Day in straw costumes and masks, playing music and collecting money. The custom is still marked in places such as Dingle.
entries.someplacessay: The dress, the songs and the way the day is kept differ from town to town.
sources: RTÉ Archives, 'Lá an Dreoilín' (Wren Day in Dingle), 17 Dec 2021, https://www.rte.ie/archives/2021/1217/1267299-la-an-dreolin, checked 2026-11-03

Anne Lucey, 'Wren Day: Those that went before us kept it going from generation to generation', The Irish Times, 27 Dec 2023, https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/2023/12/27/those-that-went-before-us-kept-it-going-from-generation-to-generation, checked 2026-11-03
entries.checkNote: Wording kept. Both sources: wren hunted and paraded on St Stephen's Day, groups in straw costumes or masks going to houses with music and collecting money; Dingle still keeps it, with four groups. The Irish Times notes it has died out in most other places.

entries.title: Nollaig na mBan, Women's Christmas
entries.text: Traditionally, 6 January was a day off housework for the women, after a busy Christmas, while the men took over the work. Women gathered informally and visited friends and neighbours. Today friends often meet for a meal or a drink.
entries.someplacessay: It is also called Little Christmas. It was well known in some areas, such as Cork and Kerry, but not everywhere, and it faded in the mid 20th century before being revived.
sources: Marion McGarry, 'The roots and traditions of Nollaig na mBan', RTÉ Brainstorm, 6 Jan 2026, https://www.rte.ie/brainstorm/2026/0106/1103975-nollaig-na-mban-january-6-ireland-roots-traditions-customs/, checked 2026-11-03
'On the woman's day of Christmas', The Irish Times, 6 Jan 1998, https://www.irishtimes.com/culture/on-the-woman-s-day-of-christmas-1.121479 (quotes Kevin Danaher on the name), checked 2026-11-03
entries.checkNote: 'Kept most strongly in Cork and Kerry' softened to 'well known in some areas such as Cork and Kerry' (RTÉ's words). Added that men taking over the work was the ideal; the Irish Times piece also stresses the heavy Christmas workload. The modern meal-or-drink line rests on general press, not these two.

entries.title: Oíche Fhéile Bríde, St Brigid's Eve
entries.text: Traditionally, on the eve of St Brigid's Day the family ate a meal of potatoes and butter and made crosses from rushes or straw in honour of the saint, asking her protection for the household, farm and land.
entries.someplacessay: The cross takes many forms: diamond, interlaced or wheel-shaped, with two, three or four arms, and other materials such as grass or wood were also used. In parts of Connacht a family member called Brigid brought in the rushes.
sources: National Museum of Ireland, 'St Brigid's Day' (curator Clodagh Doyle), https://www.museum.ie/en-ie/collections-research/folklife-collections/folklife-collections-list-(1)/religion-and-calendar-customs/st-brigid-s-day (via source.museum.ie), checked 2026-11-03

National Museum of Ireland, 'St Brigid's Crosses', https://www.museum.ie/en-IE/Collections-Research/Folklife-Collections/Folklife-Collections-List-(1)/Religion-and-Calendar-Customs/St-Brigid-s-Crosses (via source.museum.ie), checked 2026-11-03
entries.checkNote: Both sources are from the same museum (Irish Folklife Division), so they are not independent. A second independent source is still needed: the Dept of Culture's Intangible Heritage inventory page on weaving a St Brigid's cross confirms rushes, 1 February and protection, but my fetch of it was unreliable, so I have not counted it. Draft's 'hung in the house for protection' was softened to 'protection for household, farm and land' (museum's wording of purpose).

entries.title: Imbolc, Lá Fhéile Bríde
entries.text: 1 February is St Brigid's Day, and Imbolc is the old quarter day linked with the start of spring. St Brigid's Day became a public holiday in 2023, on the first Monday of February, or on 1 February itself when that falls on a Friday.
entries.someplacessay: Scholars still debate what the word Imbolc means, and St Brigid's Day is often thought to have taken over from an older pre-Christian festival. Met Éireann counts spring from 1 March (Nick Scroxton, Maynooth University, RTÉ Brainstorm, 27 Feb 2026).
sources: Organisation of Working Time (Covid-19 Commemoration) Regulations 2022, S.I. No. 50 of 2022, Irish Statute Book, https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2022/si/50/made/en/html (made 7 Feb 2022; regs 4 and 5), checked 2026-11-03

Kelly Fitzgerald (UCD), 'What do we know about the roots of the Imbolc spring festival?', RTÉ Brainstorm, 31 Jan 2024, https://www.rte.ie/brainstorm/2024/0131/1429455-imbolc-imbolg-spring-pagan-festival-brigit/, checked 2026-11-03
entries.checkNote: The draft said the holiday came from the 'Public Holidays (St Brigid's Day) Act 2022'. I could not find an Act of that name: the holiday was set by S.I. 50/2022, under the Organisation of Working Time Act 1997 (the same instrument that added 18 March 2022). The first Monday / Friday rule is exactly as drafted. 'Once separate then grew together' replaced by what the UCD scholar says: Brigid's Day is often seen as replacing Imbolc, and the word's meaning is disputed.

entries.title: Candlemas
entries.text: 2 February is Candlemas, the Feast of the Presentation of the Lord, forty days after Christmas. In many parishes candles are blessed at Mass on the day.
entries.someplacessay: Parishes differ in how they mark it, and Candlemas has long been linked with St Brigid's Day and with St Blaise the next day.
sources: Kelly Fitzgerald (UCD), 'What do we know about the roots of the Imbolc spring festival?', RTÉ Brainstorm, 31 Jan 2024, https://www.rte.ie/brainstorm/2024/0131/1429455-imbolc-imbolg-spring-pagan-festival-brigit/ (Candlemas = Presentation, 40 days after birth), checked 2026-11-03

Redemptorists Limerick, 'February 2nd: Feast of the Presentation of the Lord', https://www.redemptoristslimerick.ie/february-2nd-feast-of-the-presentation-of-the-lord/ (candles blessed at Masses on the day), checked 2026-11-03
entries.checkNote: Draft's 'some places keep Christmas decorations up until this day' is not in either source, so it is replaced. The second source is one religious community's notice: other Irish parishes (Newmarket-on-Fergus, Tralee Dominicans) say the same, but I did not read those pages in full, so I have not listed them.

entries.title: St Blaise's Day
entries.text: On 3 February, the feast of St Blaise, many parishes offer the blessing of throats: two candles are blessed, held crossed and touched against the throat while a prayer is said, asking protection from throat illness.
entries.someplacessay: Practice varies by parish. The blessing is linked with the day after Candlemas, and at the Carmelite church on Whitefriar Street in Dublin crowds attend.
sources: Erin Fox, 'The blessing of St Blaise', The Irish Catholic, 29 Jan 2015, https://www.irishcatholic.com/the-blessing-of-st-blaise/, checked 2026-11-03
RTÉ Archives, 'Blessing Of Throats - The Feast Of St Blaise 1969', https://www.rte.ie/archives/2024/0203/1428138-blessing-of-throats/, checked 2026-11-03
entries.checkNote: Draft said some parishes hold it on the nearest Sunday: not in either source, so removed. Also the sources say 'two candles touched on the throat', crossed over and pressed to either side, and say the feast is on 3 February. 'Protect against throat illness' is the healing association with St Blaise, from both.

entries.title: Lá Fhéile Pádraig, St Patrick's Day
entries.text: A national feast day and public holiday. For hundreds of years people wore crosses for the saint, and later adults wore a sprig of shamrock while children wore paper or fabric crosses, which became today's rosettes.
entries.someplacessay: The big parades are fairly modern: from the mid-19th century temperance societies held parades on the day, and it only became a national holiday in 1903.
sources: National Museum of Ireland, Irish Folklife Collections: 'St. Patrick', https://www.museum.ie/en-IE/Collections-Research/Folklife-Collections/Folklife-Collections-List-(1)/Religion-and-Calendar-Customs/St-Patrick (via source.museum.ie; Thomas Dineley 1681, children's crosses, 1908 rosettes), checked 2026-11-03

Marion McGarry, 'A day off from Lent: St Patrick's Day traditions from the past', RTÉ Brainstorm, 5 Mar 2025, https://www.rte.ie/brainstorm/2025/0305/1036394-a-day-off-from-lent-st-patricks-day-traditions-from-the-past/, checked 2026-11-03
entries.checkNote: Draft's 'older custom was church in the morning and a quiet day' is not in either source (RTÉ says the day was a welcome break from Lenten fasting), so it is replaced by what both say about badges and parades. The draft's paper cross was a child's custom, not general. The 'public holiday' status today is not in these two: RTÉ gives 1903 as when it became a national holiday.

entries.title: Cónocht an Earraigh, spring equinox
entries.text: Day and night are close to equal length, and from here the days run longer than the nights until the autumn equinox.
entries.someplacessay: The exact moment falls on 20 or 21 March, depending on the year. In 2026 it was 20 March.
sources: U.S. Naval Observatory, Astronomical Applications Department, seasons service, https://aa.usno.navy.mil/api/seasons?year=2026 (copy in test/fixtures/usno-seasons.json, fetched 2026-11-03), checked 2026-11-03

Royal Museums Greenwich, 'Space and astronomy highlights 2026', https://www.rmg.co.uk/stories/space-astronomy/space-astronomy-highlights-2026 (spring equinox 20 March; roughly equal day and night), checked 2026-11-03
entries.checkNote: Wording kept. The 'days longer than nights until autumn equinox' line follows from the definition (RMG explains the tilt). Met Éireann's own page did not load for me; Met uses 1 March for the start of spring (see the Imbolc card).

entries.title: Lady Day
entries.text: 25 March, the feast of the Annunciation, was one of the traditional quarter days for paying rents and settling accounts.
entries.someplacessay: Quarter days differed between regions and between legal and farming use.
sources: A legal or history reference on the English and Irish quarter days (to check)
Church calendar date, 25 March (to check)

entries.title: Bealtaine, May Day
entries.text: Traditionally a May bush was decorated and set up near the house, yellow flowers such as primroses were laid on doorsteps, and fires were lit to protect people and animals as summer began.
entries.someplacessay: Some places keep the old May Day on 12 May, and the flowers and customs vary by district.
sources: A folklore archive or national museum page on May Day customs (to check)
An Irish-language dictionary entry for Bealtaine (to check)

entries.title: Grianstad an tSamhraidh, summer solstice
entries.text: The longest day of the year. In most of Ireland there are around 17 hours of daylight, with true darkness hardly arriving in the far north.
entries.someplacessay: The solstice falls on 20 or 21 June, depending on the year.
sources: An astronomical almanac for the exact date (to check)
Met Éireann or Armagh Observatory page on the solstices (to check)

entries.title: Oíche Fhéile Eoin, St John's Eve
entries.text: On the eve of St John's Day, bonfires are traditionally lit, a custom still kept in parts of the south and west of Ireland.
entries.someplacessay: In some places people once drove cattle past the embers, and the fires are still strongest in certain parishes.
sources: A folklore archive entry on St John's Eve bonfires (to check)
A local-history source from a county that keeps the custom (to check)

entries.title: Lúnasa, Lughnasa
entries.text: 1 August is Lughnasa, the old quarter day that opens the harvest season. The Irish name for the month of August, Lúnasa, comes from it, and Brian Friel's play Dancing at Lughnasa takes its name from the festival.
entries.someplacessay: Gatherings on hilltops around this time of year were traditionally common, and the exact day kept differs by place.
sources: An Irish-language dictionary entry for Lúnasa (to check)
A published listing for Dancing at Lughnasa (to check)

entries.title: Puck Fair opens
entries.text: Each year, from 10 to 12 August, Killorglin in County Kerry holds Puck Fair, in which a wild mountain goat is crowned King Puck and raised above the town.
entries.someplacessay: People tell different stories about how the custom began.
sources: The Puck Fair official site (to check)
A Kerry tourism or heritage page on Puck Fair (to check)

entries.title: Lá Fhéile Muire sa Fhómhar, Assumption
entries.text: The feast of the Assumption on 15 August is a holy day, and it was a traditional day for pilgrimages and for visiting holy wells.
entries.someplacessay: Different places keep their own pattern day, and some on dates around it.
sources: Church calendar date, 15 August (to check)
A heritage page on holy wells and pattern days (to check)

entries.title: Cónocht an Fhómhair, autumn equinox
entries.text: Day and night are close to equal again, and from here the nights run longer than the days until the spring equinox.
entries.someplacessay: The exact moment falls on 22 or 23 September, depending on the year.
sources: An astronomical almanac for the exact date (to check)
Met Éireann or Armagh Observatory page on the equinoxes (to check)

entries.title: Michaelmas
entries.text: The feast of St Michael, 29 September, was traditionally marked with a goose dinner. A well-known saying warned against picking blackberries after this date.
entries.someplacessay: Some places say the blackberries are spoiled after Michaelmas, others say after Hallowe'en.
sources: Folklore archive entries on Michaelmas customs (to check)
Church calendar date, 29 September (to check)

entries.title: Is fearr an tsláinte ná na táinte
entries.text: A familiar proverb: health is better than wealth. It is often said at New Year, when people wish each other well. It is not tied to this date.
entries.someplacessay: People pronounce and write it in a few ways across different regions.
sources: An Irish proverbs collection (to check)
An English-Irish dictionary entry for sláinte (to check)

entries.title: St Valentine's Day
entries.text: Relics said to be those of St Valentine have been kept in the Carmelite church on Whitefriar Street in Dublin since the 1800s, and couples visit the shrine on 14 February.
entries.someplacessay: The church describes the relics as a gift from the Pope, and historians disagree about which St Valentine they belong to.
sources: The Whitefriar Street Carmelite church website (to check)
A history or heritage feature on the Valentine relics in Dublin (to check)

entries.title: Oíche Bhealtaine, May Eve
entries.text: May Eve was traditionally seen as a night when the fairies were active, and people took small precautions, such as keeping fire and milk in the house, to protect the household and the animals.
entries.someplacessay: The precautions differ between regions, and in some places the same beliefs attach to November Eve.
sources: Folklore archive entries on May Eve beliefs (to check)
A heritage overview of fairy lore and the calendar (to check)

entries.title: Lá Fhéile Colmcille, St Columba
entries.text: 9 June is the feast of St Columba, or Colmcille, who founded monasteries in Derry and Durrow and later the community on Iona.
entries.someplacessay: Some sources give slightly different dates for his life, though the feast day is firmly kept on 9 June.
sources: An Irish saints calendar or church calendar (to check)
A biography entry for Colmcille in a national dictionary of biography (to check)

entries.title: Lá Fhéile Chiaráin, St Ciarán
entries.text: 9 September is the feast of St Ciarán, the founder of the monastery at Clonmacnoise on the Shannon in County Offaly.
entries.someplacessay: Pilgrims have gathered at Clonmacnoise on or near his feast day, and the exact customs have varied over time.
sources: An Irish saints calendar or church calendar (to check)
A heritage page on Clonmacnoise (to check)

entries.title: The first day of winter, by the weather forecasters
entries.text: Met Éireann counts winter as December, January and February, so 1 December is the first day of winter for the weather records, even though the old Irish year began its winter a month earlier, on 1 November.
entries.someplacessay: Almanacs and many people still count winter from the shortest-day solstice, so three different starting points are in use.
sources: Met Éireann's page on the meteorological seasons (to check)
A second reference on the Irish seasons and the quarter days (to check)
